Why this catalog

Problems engineers face

Engineers are often asked to reproduce what a program does when its source is not available to them or no longer fits: replacing a legacy tool, rebuilding a component in another language, or bringing a codebase up to the behavior of a newer release. In that situation the documentation and the program's observable behavior are the specification. The engineer chooses the language and architecture, writes the code and the build, and checks the result against the original's outputs. ProgramBench frames this as rebuilding a program from scratch. The agent receives a compiled executable and its documentation, cannot read or decompile the executable, and has no internet access. It gets no method signatures, class skeletons or requirement documents, so every design decision is the agent's own. A hidden behavioral test suite, generated by agent-driven fuzzing, compares the candidate with the original, and a task counts as resolved only when all of its tests pass. This catalog also includes repository-upgrade tasks, which apply the same black-box comparison to an existing codebase that must reach a later release's behavior.

How the tasks reproduce them

Each task gives a reference program that can be run but not read, plus documentation that may be outdated. Upgrade tasks place a repository in /app/repo and require a fixed build command, /opt/task/build.sh. Reimplementation tasks give only docs in /workspace/docs and require a source project with compile.sh that builds./executable offline in a clean container. The language is the existing one for upgrades and the agent's choice for reimplementation. Grading replays hidden recorded behaviors against the rebuilt executable and compares exit code, output and file effects. Upgrade instructions say every hidden test must pass and include tests for unchanged behavior. Reimplementation scoring is the fraction of behaviors matched. Some upgrade tasks also require a research and planning file before any edit.

Typical prompts

  • Update an existing repository to match a reference binary, with a note that docs in the repo may be outdated.
  • Preserve existing behavior while adding required changes, stated as hidden tests that cover both.
  • Write a research and plan document before editing any code, then implement.
  • Reproduce the documented behavior of a program from docs and an execute-only binary, delivered as source plus compile.sh.
  • Close with a self-check list that compares every option and subcommand of the reference against the rebuilt program.

Example 1: Build systems (Agent's choice)
Final category ProgramBench reimplementation
Domain Build, release & supply chain
Sub-domain Build systems
Language Agent's choice
Seniority Staff+
Turn count 698 (z-ai/glm-5.3-flash)
Long horizon yes

Prompt shape: A fixed template that names an execute-only reference binary and its docs, asks for a source project plus compile.sh, and ends with scoring rules and a self-comparison checklist.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)
Task context

Reproduce the documented behavior of the program in this workspace. The reference program is /opt/task-reference/executable. Its bundled documentation is available in the workspace. The task runs model commands as the non-root agent user. The reference is execute-only for that user, so it can be run but not read, copied, hard-linked, or recovered through /proc. A root model shell means the task platform did not honor the declared user and is not part of the task contract.

Required result

Write a source code project and an executable ./compile.sh. Running ./compile.sh on a fresh checkout must produce ./executable in the workspace root. The rebuilt executable must match the reference program's observable behavior, including output, exit codes, and file system effects.

You may choose the implementation language and design. You can learn the behavior from the bundled documentation and by running the reference program.

The grader checks only your submission's fresh offline build and its observable behavior. It does not assess your implementation language or how you learned the behavior. Do not include the reference executable's bytes in the submission under another name or embedded inside another file. Do not read or inspect the grader harness, hidden tests, or recorded expectations, even if a platform defect makes them accessible. During grading, the internet, package registries, the reference program, and system copies of the same tool are unavailable. Your build and executable must work without them.

Reusable input assets

When /workspace/assets exists, it contains hard-to-create reusable inputs such as media, archives, databases, or custom binary files. You may inspect, copy, or modify these inputs while recreating the program. Ordinary source and text inputs are not provided and should be created as needed.

How your work is scored

Your executable is graded by replaying many recorded behaviors of the reference program against it and scoring the fraction that match. A match always requires the same exit code and the same file system effects. Plain output and ordinary files are compared byte for byte. JSON output and JSON files are normally compared as parsed values, so insignificant whitespace and object key order do not matter unless the documentation makes formatting or ordering part of the behavior. SQLite files are compared by their logical contents. Terminal progress output is compared by its final visible text. A recorded behavior can require exact bytes when formatting or ordering is part of the documented behavior. Partial credit is the norm, so every additional behavior you match raises your score, and there is no bonus for finishing early.

Coverage to aim for

Grading samples behavior from the documented interface. Only behavior that can be tested reliably in a bounded offline run is graded.

When applicable, support:

  • commands, subcommands, options, aliases, and short forms
  • representative documented values
  • help and version output
  • standard input, files, and directories
  • configuration files and environment variables
  • standard output, standard error, exit codes, and file system effects
  • error handling
  • empty, non-ASCII, binary, and unusually named inputs

The test suite may not cover every documented behavior.

Using the reference program

Run /opt/task-reference/executable to observe the reference. The file is outside the submitted workspace and is unavailable during grading. Your ./compile.sh can therefore write ./executable without replacing the reference while you work.

Before you finish

Passing tests you wrote yourself is not evidence that you are done. Before you stop:

  1. list every option and subcommand in the reference program's help output;
  2. for each one, run /opt/task-reference/executable and your executable on the same input and compare output using the scoring rules above, along with the exit code and files written;
  3. fix every disagreement you find, then repeat from step 1.

Stop when no disagreement remains or when your budget is spent, whichever comes first.

Pass rates
z-ai/glm-5.3-flash 0% 0.13

Environment

How it maps to the work

A build engineer is asked to replace a build file generator whose source is not at hand, using its manual and the installed binary. They run the tool on small Go and protobuf trees, record which BUILD.bazel files and directives it produces, and write a program that produces the same files. The work resembles porting an internal build tool to a new stack while keeping existing repositories building.

Why this catalog

Problems engineers face

Engineers in this catalog work on services where several processes share state and any of them can stop at any moment. The tasks show five recurring problems. First, duplicate effects after retries or worker restarts. Second, lost notifications when a broker or cache is down after the database commit. Third, stale writers that return after takeover. Fourth, limits and counters that hold in one process but not across instances. Fifth, partial state after a crash. The cluster tasks are system design; the single-component tasks are fault tolerance. Most specs also require that existing behaviour keeps working during the change, so a fix that blocks all writes does not pass. Time bounds such as 45 seconds after recovery turn vague reliability goals into testable ones.

How the tasks reproduce them

Each task pins a real open source repository at a base commit and gives the agent a short written spec with time bounds, such as recovery within 45 seconds. Cluster tasks supply databases, caches or brokers locally or through a compose file, and the instruction says the agent runs separate processes for each role. Docker is unavailable inside the agent container, so the agent starts local services itself. The agent produces a patch to the repository. The verifier runs in a separate environment, applies the patch and hidden tests, and kills or pauses processes and services to check the stated behaviour. The tests also check that existing behaviour listed in a keep-working section still passes.

Typical prompts

  • A production symptom with its mechanism, then a bulleted list of measurable requirements with time limits.
  • A missing capability stated in the form 'X cannot do Y', followed by dense behavioural paragraphs.
  • A story-style problem report from a team, then 'To close this out' requirements.
  • A requirements list plus an explicit list of exported names and signatures to implement.
  • A closing environment paragraph giving the repo path, service start commands, build command and the note that Docker is unavailable.

Example 1: Collaborative documents (TypeScript)
Final category System design
Domain Applications & business domains
Sub-domain Collaborative documents
Language TypeScript
Seniority Staff+
Turn count 556 (z-ai/glm-5.3-flash)
Long horizon yes

Prompt shape: A failure scenario described as current behaviour, then outcome requirements with a configured lease value, followed by a keep-working paragraph and a setup paragraph.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)
Fenced failover for document workers

We need documents served by a stopped or partitioned document worker to move to another worker, without the old worker overwriting edits if it comes back. Today such a worker keeps its Redis assignments after its liveness report expires, so requests to those documents hang, and simply reassigning them would let the old worker overwrite edits when it resumes.

What we need
  • With GRIST_DOC_WORKER_LEASE_SECONDS=3, a worker that no longer renews its lease relinquishes its documents on the next home-server lookup. Another available worker serves the last flushed document and accepts edits. Concurrent lookups from two home servers agree on one owner and do not duplicate the document.
  • A worker reporting within its lease retains its assignments.
  • An old worker resuming after takeover refuses actions from its existing websocket clients and cannot publish another document state or overwrite its checksum. An upload started before takeover but completed afterward cannot become the current document, even if the new owner has already saved edits.
Keep working

Normal document reads and edits on multiple workers, the existing worker lookup and GET /status, and coordinated moves through POST /api/docs/:docId/assign that retain flushed edits. Healthy assignments stay stable across home servers and distribute documents across available workers.

Setup

The checkout is at /app. Redis, PostgreSQL and a versioned S3-compatible object store are available through REDIS_URL, TYPEORM_* and GRIST_DOCS_S3_*. Home and doc workers are separate processes from this build (GRIST_SERVERS=home or GRIST_SERVERS=docs). The solver container has no Docker daemon or internet; dependencies are installed. Run TypeScript builds from /app with yarn run build.

Pass rates
z-ai/glm-5.3-flash 20% 0.20

Environment

How it maps to the work

An engineer operating a multi-worker document service has a stopped worker that keeps its Redis assignments, so requests hang, and a naive reassignment would let the old worker overwrite edits on resume. The engineer must add lease-based takeover and fence the stale worker at the websocket, state publication and upload paths.

Example 2: Filesystems (Go)
Final category Fault tolerance
Domain Systems, hardware & accelerators
Sub-domain Filesystems
Language Go
Seniority Staff+
Turn count 295 (z-ai/glm-5.3-flash)
Long horizon yes

Prompt shape: A capability gap stated in one sentence, dense behavioural requirements, then an explicit list of exported names and signatures the solution must provide.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)

go-diskfs cannot make crash-recoverable FAT metadata changes on whole disks or numbered partitions. Implement transactions for FAT12, FAT16, and FAT32 so committed mutations survive reopening completely, while rollback or interruption restores the prior coherent filesystem state. Make filesystem tree copying publish one recoverable destination outcome without changing established successful-copy behavior.

Rollback or interruption restores every touched allocation entry exactly, and overlapping transactions on one filesystem cannot publish conflicting outcomes or displace the active transaction. Reject unrepresentable clusters and values without writing bytes, and make durable state authoritative before reporting success. Include file, directory, allocation-chain, mirrored-table, and FAT32 free-space metadata in one outcome. Keep FAT12 and FAT16 fixed-root behavior without FSInformationSector writes.

Make recovery idempotent. Validate records against the selected filesystem geometry, never touch neighboring bytes, and return a coherent view before disk opening completes. Preserve existing probing errors, rename matching and replacement behavior, copy exclusions, contents, structure, timestamp handling, and label handling: an ordinary SetLabel made outside any transaction stays durable after the image is reopened. Keep existing exported signatures and concrete return types unchanged; in particular FileSystem.OpenFile continues to return a concrete *fat12.File.

Atomic copying must expose the complete reachable destination tree after reopening through Disk.GetFilesystem, or restore exactly the preceding tree after any source or destination failure. Nested directories and files must commit as one reachable tree.

Package github.com/diskfs/go-diskfs/filesystem/fat12 exports TransactionState, FATTransaction, ErrTransactionActive, RecoveryDisposition, and RecoveryReport; ErrTransactionActive reports exactly "FAT transaction already active". Package github.com/diskfs/go-diskfs/disk exposes Disk.RecoverFAT, and github.com/diskfs/go-diskfs/sync exposes CopyTransactionResult and CopyFileSystemAtomic. Disk.RecoverFAT returns an error, and writes no bytes, when the selected whole disk or partition holds no recognized FAT filesystem.

A FAT12 transaction spanning adjacent packed entries must reopen with byte-exact rollback or identical committed mirrored tables after durable synchronization. Interrupted file growth must restore the prior contents, length, allocation chain, and mirror agreement. Reject a malformed FAT32 transaction for incompatible partition geometry before changing reserved entries or neighboring partition bytes. Interrupted FAT32 commit recovery must leave allocation entries and FSInformationSector free-space hints describing the same durable outcome.

These are required in what you deliver:

  • TransactionState: TransactionActive = iota, TransactionCommitted, TransactionRolledBack
  • FATTransaction: SetCluster(cluster uint32, value uint32) error; Commit() error; Rollback() error; State() TransactionState
  • (fs *FileSystem) BeginFATTransaction() (FATTransaction, error)
  • (fs *FileSystem) RecoverFATTransaction() (RecoveryReport, error)
  • ErrTransactionActive = errors.New("FAT transaction already active")
  • RecoveryDisposition: RecoveryNone = iota, RecoveryRolledBack, RecoveryCompleted
  • RecoveryReport{Disposition RecoveryDisposition}
  • (d *Disk) RecoverFAT(partition int) (fat12.RecoveryReport, error)
  • CopyTransactionResult{State fat12.TransactionState}
  • CopyFileSystemAtomic(src fs.FS, dst *fat12.FileSystem) (CopyTransactionResult, error)

Pass rates
z-ai/glm-5.3-flash 75% 0.75

Environment

How it maps to the work

An engineer maintaining a filesystem library needs FAT12, FAT16 and FAT32 metadata changes to survive a crash. They must add transactions with rollback and idempotent recovery, validate records against partition geometry, and make tree copying publish one recoverable result.

Prompt shape: A race condition described from the mechanism, then a bulleted list of behavioural requirements with time limits, and a closing environment paragraph with build command.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)

Concurrent asset uploads can each pass the quota check using the same old usage value, after their files have already been written. A terminated API leaves an unfinished original on disk. The quota needs to remain a hard limit even while requests are still streaming.

To close this out:

  • Make the per-user quota a hard limit across separate API processes, including uploads through shared links. Count bytes while multipart POST /api/assets bodies are arriving, including bodies without a declared file size. Refuse an upload that would exceed committed usage plus in-flight bytes with a quota error (HTTP 400 or 413), leaving no asset or rejected file. An active slow stream retains its space.
  • Return space and remove unfinished originals on client abort within 5 seconds, and after an API process dies within 45 seconds, without requiring another request. Completing an upload charges its original once. GET /api/users/me reports committed usage, not in-flight bytes.
  • Permanent deletion, whether requested repeatedly by emptying trash or through duplicate AssetDelete jobs on the backgroundTask queue, releases the original's usage exactly once; trash and restore leave it charged. Uploads whose checksum matches an existing asset return the existing id without charging twice. Users with no quota remain unrestricted.
  • Admin quota updates and UserSyncUsage jobs cannot erase in-flight space; finishing concurrent uploads charges their accepted bytes exactly.

Work in /app (Immich at the pinned revision). PostgreSQL with VectorChord, Valkey/Redis and the shared /data upload directory are available through DB_HOSTNAME=postgres, DB_USERNAME=postgres, DB_PASSWORD=postgres, DB_DATABASE_NAME=immich, and REDIS_HOSTNAME=redis. Build with pnpm --filter immich build from /app. api and microservices run as separate workers via IMMICH_WORKERS_INCLUDE; Docker is unavailable inside the agent container.

Pass rates

Why this catalog

Problems engineers face

Engineers who maintain libraries and backends are handed behaviour that is wrong in many small places and have to find the causes without a safety net. In the diagnosis tasks the repository has lost its tests and a block of symptoms describes many unrelated failures at once. In the spec-drift tasks the code still runs but contradicts its own README and docstrings. A third pattern is a single production symptom with a hidden root cause. Across all three, the engineer must reproduce the symptom, localize the faulty function, repair it without breaking neighbouring behaviour, and in many tasks say where the defect was.

How the tasks reproduce them

Each task ships a pinned checkout of a real open-source project, with network disabled at run time and the tests removed or stubbed in the agent's tree. The prompt gives symptoms or a documentation scope but not the location of the faults. The diagnosis tasks ask for /app/rca.json listing file and function per edit, and a separate verifier container restores hidden tests and compares the report to an answer key. The spec-drift tasks keep the documentation as the authority and forbid editing it; the grader runs sealed cases as an unprivileged user and checks that the documentation is unchanged. Rewards combine fail-to-pass repairs with pass-to-pass regressions. Stated fault counts range from 4 in one task to 30 in several blind tasks.

Typical prompts

  • A first-person list of observed symptoms with a stated number of undocumented edits and a request for /app/rca.json.
  • Symptom paragraphs grouped by feature with no file or function named, ending in a fix-and-report request.
  • A repository description with an explicit in-scope and out-of-scope file list and the rule that documentation is authoritative and must not be edited.
  • A short generic request to restore documented behaviour in a repository, with the docs location given.
  • A single bug report written from a production symptom, with no pointer to the faulty module.

Prompt shape: A short brief naming the repository and the documentation in scope, stating that documentation wins over code, forbidding doc edits and API changes, and giving no list of the drifted behaviors.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)

The repository at /workdir is TanStack Form, a TypeScript library for managing form state and validation across UI frameworks.

Fix all implementation drift from the documentation in this repository. The @tanstack/form-core subsystem is specified by the API reference under docs/reference and the documentation comments in packages/form-core/src.

Where the code and the documentation disagree about runtime behavior, the documentation is the authority: change the implementation so that it does what the documentation says, and do not edit or delete documentation to make a disagreement go away. The documentation is those pages and the JSDoc comments, including their examples; in-package code comments are only supporting evidence, and when a comment conflicts with the documentation, follow the documentation.

The repository is at /workdir. The environment runs TypeScript on Node.js 24 with the repository's dependencies installed, and has no network access. Keep the public API stable and keep every behavior that already matches its documentation working exactly as it does now.

Prompt shape: Four prose symptom reports written from the caller's point of view, with no file or function named, followed by a request to fix them and list the responsible functions in rca.json.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)
libexpat: diagnosing four real defects without a test suite

I set a maximum tolerated amplification factor and an activation threshold on a parser, then created a child parser for external entity content and handed that child a lone parameter entity declaration longer than the threshold I had chosen. Parsing came back successful every time; no limit breach was ever reported, however far below the length of the declaration I pushed the threshold.

I registered a comment handler that records the comment text and then asks the parser to stop, parsed a document whose element content references an entity that in turn expands to two further levels of nested entities, and looped calling resume until parsing finished. The recorded comments stopped partway: the text following the innermost entity reference, including the trailing comments of the two enclosing entities and the material after them, never arrived.

After feeding the parser one short chunk in a non-final call, I prepared to feed it a next chunk whose length is close to the largest value a signed int can hold. The parser agreed to take it and gave me room for it, instead of refusing with an out-of-memory indication, although a request that large cannot be met.

I fed the parser a document whose declaration carries a version pseudo-attribute with nothing at all between the quotes. The parser took it without complaint and carried on to the root element, instead of stopping and reporting an error about the declaration.

There are four separate defects in the source of libexpat behind the behaviour above, each in a different function. This checkout has no test suite.

Fix the behaviour described above.

Record the functions that contain those defects in /app/rca.json, one entry each:

{
  "causes": [
    {
      "file": "expat/lib/xmlrole.c",
      "function": "enclosing_function_name"
    }
  ]
}

file is the path of the file relative to the repository root, written exactly as it appears in the tree. A file inside a directory keeps its directory prefix: the example above is expat/lib/xmlrole.c, not xmlrole.c. An absolute path, or a path with a .. segment, does not name a file in the repository and counts as a wrong entry.

function is the name of the C function whose code is wrong: the function a fix of that defect belongs in. A function defined through a macro may be named by the name the macro expands to or by the name passed to the macro. Name every function one of the defects is in, and only those, once each: a second entry for a function another entry already names, or an entry for a function that holds none of the defects, counts as a wrong entry. Where you wrote your fix does not matter: if you worked around a defect from a caller or from a helper of your own, name the function that holds the wrong code rather than the one you changed. If you suspect a function but found nothing wrong in it, leave it out.

Prompt shape: A production complaint written as a ticket (diverged runs sort first in a sweep CSV while the live view shows NaN), with no module named, asking for a source-level fix, a regression test and a root-cause note in rca.json.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)

Diverged runs come out on top of our sweep CSV

We run our hyperparameter sweeps in local mode with the CSVWriter plugin and pick the winner by sorting swanlab_runs.csv on the final val/loss. The runs that blew up near the end (loss going to NaN in the last epochs) show up in that CSV with a val/loss of 0.0, so they sort straight to the top. We only caught it because last week's "best" learning rate turned out to have diverged. In swanlab watch the same runs do end in NaN, like they should.

The checkout is in /workdir. Could you track down where this actually goes wrong and fix it there? Please include a regression test, somewhere under tests/ (say tests/test_repro.py), that fails on the current code because of this problem (a real test failure, not an import error) and passes once it's fixed. Test the reported behaviour, not your patch: it should still pass if the bug gets fixed some other correct way, so no asserting on source text or on helpers only your fix has. It should run on its own from a clean checkout with just your test files added.

I doubt I'm the only one hitting this. Anything else that goes through that code is probably wrong too, so please fix it at the source rather than special-casing my input. The fix belongs in the library itself, not in the tests. CI runs the full test suite on every change, so it shouldn't break anything else.

When you're done, leave a short root-cause note at /workdir/rca.json:

{
  "root_causes": [{"file": "path/from/repo/root.py", "function": "Class.method"}],
  "reproducer": "tests/test_repro.py"
}

root_causes lists the function(s) where the problem actually starts (one or more), not where it shows up: the file relative to the repo root and the name as function or Class.method. Don't pad the list with functions that only pass the bad value along; extra entries count against the note. reproducer is the repo-relative path of your regression test.

Why this catalog

Problems engineers face

Engineers in the catalog's main roles, such as library, backend and developer tools engineers, add a capability to an existing library or service and must leave unconfigured behavior unchanged. The tasks show four recurring patterns. One is an opt-in subsystem that spans many code paths with one shared model. A second is bounded or safe handling of untrusted input. A third is restoring stubbed functions that currently panic or throw. A fourth is concurrency and lifecycle correctness. Fixing a fail-open defect is also present in one task. Across all four, the engineer reads a large unfamiliar codebase, matches names and signatures given in the brief, and keeps existing tests passing.

How the tasks reproduce them

Each task gives the agent a pinned repository inside an offline container and a written specification. The two provided tasks show the range. The Java example ships a pre-laid data layer and a Maven cache, and its instruction names methods, error types and a rollback rule. The Go example ships a library with panicking stubs and lists banned imports and calls. The agent's edits are collected as a git diff against a base commit. Grading runs hidden tests after the session, outside the agent's view, and for the minab task the verifier runs from a root-owned copy of the base repository so the session cannot alter it. Existing tests must also keep passing.

Typical prompts

  • A capability gap stated as 'X cannot Y', then a list of exact type names, signatures and edge-case rules, ending with a clause to preserve behavior when the feature is unused. Example.
  • A first-person request to restore methods that currently panic or throw 'not implemented', named by file. Example.
  • A compact feature brief tied to one product area, with a final step that removes or replaces an old API. Example.
  • A short imperative request with exposed API signatures and a constraint such as no new crates. Example.
  • A security-flavored defect report that asks for a corrected behavior and a regression guarantee. Example.

Prompt shape: A dense feature specification that names the target service method, the exact fields and error types, a transactional rollback rule, and a final instruction to remove the old API while keeping existing tests green.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)

Loan accounts can still be opened bare: LoanAccountService.createLoanAccount(UUID, String), behind POST /api/v1/loan-accounts, opens an account with no guarantors or collateral and leaves the borrower's other applications pending. Make createSecuredLoanAccount(SecuredOriginationRequest) the only way to open one.

In one transaction it should:

  • open the account from the approved application with today's checks and product terms (IllegalArgumentException on failure);
  • attach every requested guarantor (customer, type, amount) and collateral item (all CollateralRequest details);
  • set territoryCode and originationReference = <territoryCode>/<lead guarantor customer id>/<account number>, where the lead (leadGuarantorCustomerId) must be an INDIVIDUAL guarantor, or CORPORATE for a corporateGroup, else IllegalArgumentException;
  • withdraw the borrower's other pending applications, or the group's (applicant plus groupCustomerIds), through LoanApplicationService, pointing them at the account and leaving everything else untouched;
  • write one LoanOriginationAudit (application, analyst, territory, group flag, withdrawn count).

A rejected request saves nothing.

Then retire the bare path: remove createLoanAccount(UUID, String) and LoanAccountCreateRequest, and have POST /api/v1/loan-accounts take a SecuredOriginationRequest and still answer 201 with the account. All existing loan-service tests must pass (mvn -pl loan/loan-service -am test); don't edit the poms.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)

I'm restoring transaction and query support in our copy of go-memdb so callers can update data, query snapshots, and watch query results for updates. Could you implement the methods that currently panic in the root memdb package? They live in txn.go, memdb.go, index.go, filter.go, and watch.go. The missing pieces cover transaction lifecycle, deletion, indexed queries and iteration, snapshots, deferred callbacks, filtering, and watch sets.

The existing code, API comments, and README.md provide context for the restoration. A received value must wake WatchCtx just as a closed watched channel does. Please keep the restored public names and signatures unchanged, and retain Txn.write for package compatibility; private helper functions are up to you. I'll check the restored behavior alongside index and schema regressions. Submit text Go source changes without new symbolic links, binary Go diffs, or Go line-position directives (//line and /*line). Use Go filenames that produce unquoted, whitespace-free paths in Git diffs.

In the non-test code you add, please avoid: new init() functions; the syscall, golang.org/x/sys, os/exec, os/signal, plugin, embed, runtime/cgo, runtime/pprof, runtime/trace, testing and flag packages, cgo, and //go:linkname or //go:embed directives; os.Exit, os.StartProcess, os.FindProcess and runtime.Goexit; reading os.Args, os.Executable, /proc/self or runtime/debug build info; caller or stack lookups (runtime.Caller, Callers, CallersFrames, FuncForPC, Stack, debug.Stack, debug.PrintStack, log.Lshortfile, log.Llongfile, and AddSource selectors or identifier keys); literal U+0016 or the text \x16; and printing test-runner lines such as --- PASS. These are rejected outright. Some checks read raw text and also match comments.

Why this catalog

Problems engineers face

Platform engineers in this catalog restructure infrastructure code that is already running. The most common task is a flat Terraform root module that has to become local modules with for_each keys. The change must reach production as address moves only, because the team cannot plan against a live account. A second pattern is replacing positional count with stable keys for zones, services or stages, where operations were indexed in several historical orders. A third is extracting reusable components from an app that builds everything inline, where synthesized output must not change. The example set adds two further problems: moving a stack between tools while a preview stays clean (the Pulumi ports) and bringing a stack under a policy pack without replacing resources.

How the tasks reproduce them

Each task ships a copy of the stack with its recorded production state or recorded templates, an offline toolchain and no network. The Terraform refactor tasks include a CI script that plans with refresh disabled and runs conftest on the plan. The instruction states module ownership, key rules, root variables with today's defaults and outputs. A separate verifier container holds its own pristine state, plans the agent's configuration, and then plans hidden changes such as an added key under a fresh name, a removed key or a changed entry. The CDK task compares synthesized templates for hidden configurations. The Pulumi tasks run previews against an imported stack and against a copy with swapped generated IDs. Most tasks score zero when a gate fails.

Typical prompts

  • A refactor request for a named production stack that lists target modules, ownership, key rules, root variables and outputs, and requires a plan of moves only.
  • A componentization request that lists every construct class with its path, props and public properties, and requires identical synthesized templates.
  • A migration brief for an imported stack with an empty program, with naming, config and equivalence rules and banned options.
  • A compliance remediation request with numbered requirements, a policy pack, a guardrail spec and an exceptions register, graded with hidden variable probes.
  • A bulleted list of needs followed by constraints to keep working, such as a clean preview and unchanged owned files.

Prompt shape: A refactor request for an IPv6 Kubernetes stack that names four target modules and constrains the result to a plan of moves against recorded state.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)

The Terraform for our dual IPv6 Kubernetes production stack in /workspace/infra has grown into one flat root module: everything is declared at the top level, the per-AZ resources are count-indexed by list position, and names, settings and tags are hard-coded all over the files. Split it into four local modules (network, bootstrap, platform and observability) without touching the running infrastructure: against the current state, the plan has to come out as nothing but moves.

There is no AWS access from this machine. terraform init works offline from the local provider mirror, terraform.tfstate is a copy of the production state, and scripts/ci-plan.sh runs what CI runs: a terraform plan -refresh=false against the state followed by the guardrail policies in policies/.

Detailed Constraints

How CI judges the change. CI takes the repository alone and plans it with terraform plan -refresh=false against its own copy of the production state. Local terraform state commands and edits to terraform.tfstate never reach it, so the whole migration has to be expressed in the configuration. That plan must:

  • still manage every resource that is in the state today, and
  • contain no create, update, replace, destroy or forget: only resources moving to new addresses.

The guardrail policies in policies/ must pass on that plan, and providers.tf and everything in policies/ stay exactly as they are, byte for byte.

Layout.

  • The root module calls module "network", module "bootstrap", module "platform" and module "observability", with sources ./modules/network, ./modules/bootstrap, ./modules/platform and ./modules/observability and one instance each, calls no other module and declares no resources of its own.
  • Which module owns what (every instance of the resources described, wherever they are declared today):
    • network: both VPCs, their internet gateways, public and workload subnets, Elastic IPs and NAT64-capable NAT gateways, route tables, IPv4 and IPv6 routes, and route table associations;
    • bootstrap: the bootstrap KMS key and alias, S3 bucket and every bucket settings resource, the per-pool bootstrap objects, the DynamoDB bootstrap table, and the network and worker SSM configuration catalogs;
    • platform: both clusters' control-plane and worker IAM roles, inline policies and instance profiles, security groups and rules, CloudWatch log groups, launch templates and auto scaling groups;
    • observability: the alert SNS topic, SQS queue, subscription and queue policy, and both clusters' per-pool capacity alarms.
  • Each of these modules declares the resources it owns itself and calls no other module.
  • Modules get each other's IDs and ARNs through module outputs and variables. Never paste an ID, ARN, IP address or DNS name of an existing resource, or any part of one (such as an ARN suffix), into the .tf files or templates. The configuration reads files only through literal paths inside its own module (such as "${path.module}/templates/..."; in a child module a path starts with ${path.module}/, because Terraform resolves any other relative path from the root directory, not from the module): no computed paths, no terraform_remote_state data sources, and never the state or a plan file.

Keys.

  • Everything that exists once per availability zone today is a for_each resource keyed by the AZ name (for example ["us-east-1a"]), including each instance of a list that also holds things that belong to no single availability zone.
  • Everything that exists once per worker pool today is a for_each resource keyed by the pool name (for example ["mesh"]), including each instance of a list that also holds things that belong to no single worker pool.
  • Don't use count anywhere. Other repeated resources use for_each with string keys that are not numbers (a name such as ["assets"], never ["0"]).
  • Each existing availability zone's entry in availability_zones is the only source of its values: changing an entry changes, for that availability zone alone, exactly the settings the entry provides, and changes nothing else.
  • Adding an availability zone to availability_zones must plan only the creation of that availability zone's resources, each configured exactly like its counterparts in the existing availability zones apart from the availability zone itself and the values its entry in availability_zones gives it (same settings, names and tags), and removing one only the destruction of that availability zone's resources. Beyond that, the only change either may plan is an in-place update of the settings that collect something from every availability zone today (wherever a setting holds a part of every availability zone: their names, IDs, ARNs, subnets or CIDRs, say, in a list, a policy document or an environment value): each of them must take in, or drop, exactly that availability zone's part where it belongs, in the same form as today (today's parts keep their order; where a new part goes is up to you), and change nothing else. No other resource may be created, updated, replaced or destroyed.
  • Each existing worker pool's entry in worker_pools is the only source of its values: changing an entry changes, for that worker pool alone, exactly the settings the entry provides, and changes nothing else.
  • Adding a worker pool to worker_pools must plan only the creation of that worker pool's resources, each configured exactly like its counterparts in the existing worker pools apart from the worker pool itself and the values its entry in worker_pools gives it (same settings, names and tags), and removing one only the destruction of that worker pool's resources. Beyond that, the only change either may plan is an in-place update of the settings that collect something from every worker pool today (wherever a setting holds a part of every worker pool: their names, IDs, ARNs, subnets or CIDRs, say, in a list, a policy document or an environment value): each of them must take in, or drop, exactly that worker pool's part where it belongs, in the same form as today (today's parts keep their order; where a new part goes is up to you), and change nothing else. No other resource may be created, updated, replaced or destroyed.

Root variables. Declare these in the root module, each defaulting to today's value:

  • project (string, "v6mesh"): every whole-word occurrence of v6mesh in a resource name, identifier or tag value today comes from it (whole word: not part of a longer run of letters and digits, so v6mesh-api, v6mesh_key and /v6mesh/ count, while a longer word that merely contains v6mesh stays as it is), and so does every mention of those names elsewhere in the configuration (for example a resource name inside a policy); inside documents such as policies, container definitions and environment values, every whole-word occurrence of v6mesh that stands for it comes from it too; This includes the PROJECT value in every launch template's user data, project fields in the SSM catalogs and bootstrap objects, and the project token in alarm namespaces and dimensions.
  • environment (string, "prod"): every whole-word occurrence of prod in a resource name, identifier or tag value today, and the ENVIRONMENT value in every launch template's user data, the environment fields in the SSM catalogs and bootstrap objects, and the environment token in alarm namespaces and dimensions, comes from it (whole word: not part of a longer run of letters and digits, so prod-api, prod_key and /prod/ count, while a longer word that merely contains prod stays as it is), and so does every mention of those names elsewhere in the configuration (for example a resource name inside a policy); inside documents such as policies, container definitions and environment values, every whole-word occurrence of prod that stands for it comes from it too.
  • primary_vpc_cidr (string, "172.20.0.0/16"): the alpha cluster VPC's IPv4 CIDR and its control-plane API security-group rule.
  • secondary_vpc_cidr (string, "172.21.0.0/16"): the beta cluster VPC's IPv4 CIDR and its control-plane API security-group rule.
  • availability_zones: map(object({ order = number, primary_public_cidr = string, primary_workload_cidr = string, secondary_public_cidr = string, secondary_workload_cidr = string })), keyed by AZ name, defaulting to today's three AZs, their stable collection order and all four subnet CIDRs. It is the only source of AZ membership, AZ order and subnet CIDRs.
  • worker_pools: map(object({ order = number, instance_type = string, disk_size = number, min_size = number, max_size = number, desired_size = number })), keyed by pool name, defaulting to today's gateway, system and mesh pools, their stable collection order, instance type, root disk size and scaling bounds. It is the only source of worker-pool membership, order and sizing.
  • tags (map(string), { Owner = "soloio-platform", CostCenter = "cc-6204", ManagedBy = "terraform" }): the shared tags (Owner, CostCenter and ManagedBy) that tagged resources carry today. Wherever the configuration writes them out today, in any form, they come from this variable, so that a different map (other keys, other values) reaches every one of those places; a resource's other tags stay as they are, and resources that are untagged today stay untagged.
  • node_ami_id (string, "ami-0009de7aaac3fdbb1"): the AMI of every control-plane and worker launch template.
  • master_instance_type (string, "t3.medium"): the instance type of both control-plane launch templates.
  • log_retention_days (number, 30): the retention period of every control-plane and worker CloudWatch log group.
  • bootstrap_version_retention_days (number, 30): the bootstrap bucket's noncurrent-version retention period.
  • alarm_period_seconds (number, 60): the metric period of every worker-pool capacity alarm.
  • Changing primary_vpc_cidr, secondary_vpc_cidr, node_ami_id, master_instance_type, log_retention_days, bootstrap_version_retention_days and alarm_period_seconds changes only what each one's line above says it controls: every other setting keeps today's value, including a setting that merely has the same value today.

Root outputs. Keep primary_vpc_id, secondary_vpc_id, bootstrap_bucket_name and alerts_topic_arn with their current values. primary_workload_subnet_ids becomes a map from the AZ name to the id of that availability zone's aws_subnet.primary_workload. secondary_workload_subnet_ids becomes a map from the AZ name to the id of that availability zone's aws_subnet.secondary_workload. primary_nat64_public_ips becomes a map from the AZ name to the public_ip of that availability zone's aws_eip.primary_nat64. secondary_nat64_public_ips becomes a map from the AZ name to the public_ip of that availability zone's aws_eip.secondary_nat64. primary_worker_asg_names becomes a map from the pool name to the name of that worker pool's aws_autoscaling_group.primary_worker. secondary_worker_asg_names becomes a map from the pool name to the name of that worker pool's aws_autoscaling_group.secondary_worker. bootstrap_object_keys is a new output: a map from the pool name to the key of that worker pool's aws_s3_object.pool_bootstrap. Each output passes through outputs of the module that owns the resource (network for primary_vpc_id, secondary_vpc_id, primary_workload_subnet_ids, secondary_workload_subnet_ids, primary_nat64_public_ips and secondary_nat64_public_ips; bootstrap for bootstrap_bucket_name and bootstrap_object_keys; platform for primary_worker_asg_names and secondary_worker_asg_names; observability for alerts_topic_arn): the root output is a plain reference to an output of that module, and that module output is a plain reference to the resource. A plain reference is a reference such as module.network.<output> or <resource type>.<name>.<attribute>, a local that holds one, or a for expression that only re-keys one ({ for k, v in <reference> : k => v.id }) or iterates a plain reference and looks each key up in one ({ for k, v in var.<map> : k => <reference>[k].id }); no literals, function calls, conditionals or string templates anywhere along the way.

Not allowed anywhere in the configuration: ignore_changes, prevent_destroy and replace_triggered_by, removed and import blocks, provisioners, external data sources, backend or cloud blocks, provider blocks other than the one in providers.tf, override files and .tf.json files.

Prompt shape: A migration brief written as a bulleted list of needs, with naming and equivalence rules, constraints on Pulumi options and the checks to keep passing.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)
Pulumi program for AtlasGrid's imported dev stack

AtlasGrid's production ECS platform is managed with Terraform (/workspace/terraform; terraform.tfstate is production). The platform team bulk-imported every production resource into stack dev of the Pulumi project /workspace/pulumi, but its entry point index.ts declares nothing, so a preview would delete everything. We need the matching TypeScript program.

What we need
  • Each module call is a pulumi.ComponentResource under the stack, named after the module and typed atlasgrid:modules:<Module> (Network, Identity, Edge, Cluster, Workloads, Observability).
  • Each Terraform resource instance is one @pulumi/aws resource under its module's component, named after the Terraform resource plus -<key> for for_each instances (ecs-us-east-1a).
  • Each variable in variables.tf is a same-named config key (atlasgrid-ecs:project, …) holding its value as plain YAML (integers, strings, mappings); unset keys take the Terraform default.
  • For any values Terraform and AWS accept, pulumi preview plans the same creates, updates, replacements, deletions, settings and outputs as terraform plan with those values.
  • Values Terraform reads from another resource's attribute come from that attribute's output (unknown in preview exactly where unknown in Terraform's plan).
  • Lists built from maps use sorted key order, and later maps win in merge().
  • If the stack state drifts, the preview reverts the drift as Terraform would.
  • Stack outputs match outputs.tf: same names and values (maps as objects).
  • Default aws provider only; no protect, ignoreChanges, retainOnDelete, deletedWith, import, aliases, replaceOnChanges, replaceWith, customTimeouts, transforms or hooks options, stack transforms, remote components, .get() lookups, StackReferences or provider functions like aws.getRegion().
  • No production-generated IDs, ARNs, account ID, IPs or DNS names anywhere in /workspace/pulumi, even partly or in notes; constants from the Terraform code are fine.
  • The program runs offline from the regular files in /workspace/pulumi alone (no symlinks).
Keep working
  • Production: pulumi preview --refresh=false on dev shows no changes
  • A clean npx tsc --noEmit
  • Pulumi.yaml, Pulumi.dev.yaml, package.json, tsconfig.json, templates/, byte for byte (undo any pulumi config set)
Setup

No AWS access; pulumi preview --refresh=false works offline (backend /workspace/pulumi-state and passphrase preset) and pulumi stack export shows every URN. In /workspace/terraform, terraform init -input=false and terraform plan -refresh=false work offline from a provider mirror, including with -var/-var-file. node_modules links to the image's packages (Node.js 22, versions per package.json; @pulumi/aws 6.83.0 is built on Terraform's AWS provider 5.100.0); nothing can be installed. templates/userdata.sh.tpl copies the cluster module's template.

Prompt shape: A componentization request that spells out every construct class with its path, props and public properties, and requires identical synthesized templates for any valid configuration.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)

The Orion accelerator CDK app builds every resource inline in three long stack constructors. Nothing in it is reusable: a stage's queue, topic, task definition, routing and alarms are just lines in one loop.

To close this out:

  • Split it into components; only tags, outputs and what aws-cdk-lib adds at a stack's root stay outside them. Each is a Construct exported from lib/components/<class-name-in-kebab-case>.ts, at the given path under its stack, props in parentheses. Props use lib/config.ts types (settings is one entry, lists are string[], stageTopics and stageQueues are plain objects keyed by stage name) and take aws-cdk-lib constructs as I interfaces (ec2.IVpc), except OperationsMonitoring's fn, a lambda.Function. Public properties are read-only, concretely typed, and fooBar is the child FooBar unless noted; <name> is the config entry's key.
  • NetworkStack: CoreNetwork at Network (cidr, maxAzs, natGateways) exposing vpc; GatewayAccess at Gateway (vpc) exposing endpoint; FlowLogging at FlowLogs (vpc, project, stage, logRetentionDays) exposing logGroup, flowLog; NetworkSecurity at Security (vpc, prefix, cidr, containerPort) exposing deliverySecurityGroup (Delivery), runtimeSecurityGroup (Runtime), notificationSecurityGroup (Notifications). The S3 gateway endpoint and the flow log hang off the VPC today; they move out from under it into GatewayAccess and FlowLogging.
  • DeliveryStack: ArtifactEncryption at Encryption (prefix) exposing key; ArtifactBucket at Buckets/<name> (name, settings, prefix, account, isProd, encryptionKey) exposing bucket; ReleaseCatalog at Releases (prefix, encryptionKey) exposing table; RuntimePlatform at Platform (prefix, vpc, isProd) exposing repository, cluster; DeliveryGateway at Gateway (vpc, securityGroup, prefix) exposing loadBalancer, its listener (LoadBalancer/HttpListener, added to the load balancer), zone (HostedZone); StageRuntime at Stages/<name> (project, environment, name, settings, prefix, image, containerPort, logRetentionDays, queueRetentionDays, encryptionKey, storageBucket, releaseTable) exposing queue (DeployQueue), topic (EventsTopic), taskDefinition, holding ServiceLogs, TaskDocument; StageRouting at Routes/<name> (name, settings, prefix, vpc, listener, loadBalancer, zone, containerPort, healthCheckPath, deregistrationSeconds) exposing blueTarget, greenTarget, record (AliasRecord), holding ListenerRule (the target groups and rule move out from under the listener); DiscoveryParameters at Parameters (project, stage, repository, loadBalancer) holding RepositoryArnParameter, LoadBalancerDnsParameter.
  • OperationsStack: NotificationChannel at Channel (prefix, encryptionKey, emails) exposing topic; NotificationProcessor at Processor (project, stage, prefix, stageNames, memoryMiB, timeoutSeconds, logRetentionDays, vpc, securityGroup, encryptionKey, channel, stageTopics, stageQueues) exposing fn (Function), holding Logs; PipelineEventRule at Rules/<name> (name, prefix, settings, topic) exposing rule; OperationsMonitoring at Monitoring (project, stage, prefix, fn, topic, stageQueues) exposing healthAlarm (Health), dashboard, holding TopicParameter, FunctionParameter.
  • For any config that fits lib/config.ts, not just prod and staging, every stack synthesizes today's template, each resource made by the same aws-cdk-lib construct class, with no raw overrides. The one change is a component tag on each owner-tagged resource inside a component, holding that component's lower-cased path under the stack (stages/dev).
  • bash scripts/ci.sh passes.

The stacks keep their signatures and public properties, and bin/accelerator.ts, lib/config.ts, the root config files, config/, lambda/, deployed/, tools/ and scripts/ stay untouched, apart from adding config/<name>.json and deployed/<name>/ to try configs.

Everything runs offline in /workspace/accelerator-platform (npx cdk synth -c stage=<stage>; see the README); git has today's app.

Why this catalog

Problems engineers face

Data engineers and analytics engineers repair pipelines and libraries after an upstream feed changes its shape. In these tasks a vendor or connector changes format and the next run produces wrong data without failing. Fivetran or Stripe exports start resending changed records, so dbt models show duplicates and stale totals. Files change encoding or layout: a sep= line in CSV, CONTINUE records in XLS, locale formats in sheets, new Parquet types. Incremental loaders mis-track state when a schema changes mid-run or a site is added. Nightly ordering and failure handling go wrong. Each report also expects results to be the same on reruns and no regression in existing tests.

How the tasks reproduce them

Each task is a public repository checked out at a pinned commit in /app, with a Python virtual environment in /opt/venv and, where needed, dbt and DuckDB. Sample inputs such as CSV, Parquet, XML, SQLite files or seeds are copied to /data or sit in the project. The agent has no network access. The prompt gives the symptom and the required behavior, but no pointer to the faulty code. After the agent finishes, a separate verifier applies the agent's diff of /app, adds hidden tests, runs the repository's own checks and the hidden suite as an unprivileged user, and grades both reports. Some prompts add lint, type or changelog requirements.

Typical prompts

  • A first person production symptom after a vendor or connector change, with a sample location in /data.
  • A behavior spec in prose with edge cases, defaults and idempotence rules, ending with a request to fix the library without breaking existing tests.
  • An opt-in feature request for a parser or loader, with defaults that must not change.
  • A format or locale decoding failure where every sample file must read exactly as written.
  • A dbt project fix that must stay in SQL models, macros and YAML and pass dbt build.

Prompt shape: An export format switch with a failing command given verbatim and an equivalence requirement between two input formats.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)

Since the night of 2026-10-04 the order platform writes its nightly export as CSV instead of JSON. That first night it wrote both, so /data/orders has orders-2026-10-04.json and orders-2026-10-04.csv with the same orders, the CSV from the next night, and our pipeline config, /data/orders/pipeline.yml. The pipeline validates and cleans the export, then summarizes the cleaned CSV. On the CSV export, etlplus run --config /data/orders/pipeline.yml --job order_summary fails validation, and with validation turned off the summary totals are wrong.

Any etlplus job that reads a CSV file should give the result it gives on the same records as JSON: every record exactly once with the same fields, and the same validation outcome, filter result, sort order and aggregate values. An empty cell is a missing value. This also holds for a job reading a CSV file that an earlier job in the run wrote. Values in the output files may stay text.

Please fix etlplus in /app. The existing tests in /app/tests and the ruff, pydocstyle, pydoclint and mypy checks the project runs in CI have to keep passing. There's no network; the project's environment is installed in /opt/venv.

Prompt shape: A numeric symptom from real data with a precise definition of correct output per edge case and lint requirements.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)

We've switched to a new tracking vendor and load their exports straight into TrackingData, like TrackingData(pd.read_csv("/data/tracking/match_2026-09-27.csv"), provider="vendor", frame_rate=25). That file is a sample of Saturday's export. The physical numbers we get from it are off. add_velocity gives players speeds of 30 m/s and more right after halftime and around short camera dropouts, so the get_covered_distance totals and speed zone distances come out too high. Also, filter_tracking_data only smooths the ball; player positions don't change at all.

A frame's values should only come from its own stretch, meaning the frames of one period with no missing frame number between them. For each stretch, add_velocity, add_acceleration and filter_tracking_data (ball and players) should give what their usual calculation gives on that stretch alone, taken in frame order. A stretch of a single frame gets NaN velocity and acceleration. When smoothing is asked for, a stretch with no more frames than the window length keeps its unsmoothed values. Data without a frame column is taken in row order with no missing frames, and data without a period_id column is one period.

ruff check and ruff format --check on /app/databallpy and /app/tests have to stay clean, and the existing tests in /app/tests should keep passing.

Could you find what's going on and fix it? There's no network here; databallpy is installed in editable mode from /app.

Prompt shape: A feature request for a widely used library, written as a list of behaviors per option with compatibility constraints for existing behavior.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)

Our partner's XML feed now carries explicit nulls and text where padding matters. A sample is in /data/partner-feed.xml. Extend the existing xmltodict.parse and xmltodict.unparse APIs in /app so callers can opt into the new feed without changing the defaults.

With parse(..., xsi_nil=True), an element whose XML Schema instance nil attribute is true or 1 becomes None, regardless of its prefix, other attributes or text. Other values of nil and ordinary empty elements keep their existing behavior. This works with namespace processing on or off, and with streaming callbacks. With parse(..., xml_space=True), xml:space="preserve" retains text and comment whitespace exactly, including whitespace only text; descendants inherit this policy until xml:space="default" restores the normal stripping rule. This also applies to streamed entries, even when the input arrives in byte chunks. The two options can be used together.

With unparse(..., xsi_nil=True), every None element, including nested elements and list entries, emits an explicit schema instance nil attribute with a valid namespace binding. Empty strings remain ordinary empty elements. A nullable document can be parsed, written and parsed again without losing its null locations. Without the new options, existing parsing and writing behavior must stay the same. Malformed XML and invalid UTF-8 still raise Expat errors, and entity declarations remain disabled by default with ValueError.

The environment has Python 3.12, installed project dependencies and no network. The existing repository checks should still pass.

Why this catalog

Problems engineers face

Engineers in the catalog's main roles remove a dependency in one language by replacing it with a port in another. In these tasks the source is Java or Rust and the target is Go, with a few C++ targets such as mamrhein/fpdec.rs, cydhra/vers, toeverything/y-octo and houseme/qrcode-rs. The recurring difficulty is exact behavioral equivalence without seeing the tests: numeric precision in dynatrace-oss/dynahist and fpdec.rs, bit-exact random sequences in commons-rng-core, parser and error-case fidelity in rust-php-parser and htmlunit-xpath, and ordering of results in rust-rrule and dagre-rs. A second difficulty is the target language's runtime rules, such as Go's RE2 regular expressions panicking at start-up, or C++ header conventions in the PORTING.md for fpdec.rs. A third is working inside house constraints on imports and naming for code that ends up in a sandboxed service. The engineer reads the original source as the specification.

How the tasks reproduce them

Each task provides the source library under /app, a skeleton in the target language with final signatures and stub bodies, and a mig-check tool that compares the skeleton, builds and vets the port. The tests of the original project, translated to the target language, are withheld and run in a separate container after the session. The agent's edits are collected as a git diff against a tagged base commit. The instruction states per-test time and memory limits and bans some standard packages. In the provided tasks a manifest lists the required tests, and the grader module records a reward from the passing results.

Typical prompts

  • A first-person request to port a named library or crate to Go from a reference folder, with a stub skeleton and withheld tests. Example.
  • A request framed by a business reason for the move, such as retiring a JVM dependency, with emphasis on exact reproduction of seeded output. Example.
  • A request for a C++ port because a tool cannot link Rust, with a pointer to a PORTING.md that lists house rules for headers. Example.
  • A structured prompt with a title, a list of provided inputs, a how-to-work section and a statement that hidden tests grade the port. Example.
  • A bullet list of language-specific pitfalls, such as RE2 regular expression syntax and reserved name prefixes. Example.

Prompt shape: A first-person request to port a named library to Go from a source directory, with stubbed signatures given and the tests withheld, followed by a bullet list of build, naming and import rules.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)

We're moving a dependency from Rust to Go, and I need a Go port of the kookyleo/dagre-rs crate. The Rust source is in /app/rust_reference/. I've already laid out the Go package in /app/port/: every type and function our code calls is there with its final signature, but the bodies are just stubs. Could you fill in the implementation so it behaves exactly like the Rust crate?

When you're done, I'll run the crate's own test suite, ported to Go, against /app/port. I'm not including those tests here, so please work from the Rust source itself and match it closely: error cases, edge cases, numeric precision and the order things come back in.

A few things that will save you some pain:

  • Keep the signatures and the package name in /app/port as they are; our callers use them as-is. Edit the existing files in place and declare each type and function once.
  • Run mig-check (on the PATH) often. It compares /app/port with the original stubs, runs go build and go vet, and flags package-level names that clash with our test helpers (they start with mig or Mig).
  • Go's regexp is RE2, so Rust-only syntax such as the (?u) flag, \u{...} escapes, back-references and look-around makes a package-level regexp.MustCompile panic at start-up.
  • This package ends up inside a sandboxed service, so every non-test .go file under /app/port must stay off os, os/exec, syscall, runtime, plugin, net, net/http, net/rpc, io/ioutil, embed, unsafe, flag or testing (and anything under testing/), cgo, and the //go:linkname and //go:embed directives. Write the logic yourself rather than calling out to another program; the rest of the standard library is fine.
  • Our test machine has 2 vCPUs, and each test gets 60 seconds and a 2 GB address-space limit, so keep things reasonably efficient.

Pass rates
x-ai/grok-4.7 38% 0.38
google/gemini-4-argon 50% 0.50

How it maps to the work
